stories.title: Vocus hit by Australia Singapore Cable break in Indonesian waters
stories.summary: Vocus has reported a fault on the Australia Singapore Cable after a break occurred in Indonesian waters, disrupting capacity on the subsea route connecting Australia and Southeast Asia. Traffic has been rerouted while repair operations are arranged, with vessel availability and permit requirements in Indonesian waters typically dictating restoration timelines.
stories.why_it_matters: Cable breaks in busy and permit-heavy waters like Indonesia's can take weeks to repair, testing network redundancy for carriers and cloud customers. The incident underscores the fragility of Australia-Asia connectivity and the growing importance of route diversity.
stories.content:
## Key points

- Vocus is grappling with a cable break on its Australia Singapore Cable (ASC) system between Perth and Singapore, following a shunt fault on the second major cable on the route weeks earlier.
- COTDR testing from the Perth cable landing station has pinpointed the break to Indonesian waters between Anyer and Singapore, with Vocus now coordinating marine repairs, spare materials and regulatory approvals.
- Internet traffic has been rerouted via alternate paths, with network engineers on Reddit reporting traffic shifting to Australian east coast cables and then through Japan or the United States.

Vocus is dealing with a break on its Australia Singapore Cable (ASC) system that runs between Perth and Singapore, weeks after the second major cable on the route experienced a shunt fault.

The problems with ASC began Friday night and were traced to a cable break between Anyer, which sits about 80km west of Jakarta, and Singapore, in Indonesian waters.

Vocus said in status updates that coherent optical time domain reflectometry (COTDR) testing from its Perth cable landing station had provided a more “accurate measurement of the cable break location.”

”[We are] working closely with its marine repair partner to progress repair readiness, including reviewing the latest diagnostic results, confirming the required spare materials, and coordinating the necessary permits and regulatory approvals,” it said in its most recent status update.

The transmission operator said that internet traffic had been “rerouted via alternate paths”.

What this means will vary by internet service provider or other organisations that rely on west coast subsea paths to route traffic to Singapore and beyond.

But network engineers posting to Reddit indicated that traffic was rerouting to cables on Australian east coast, and then via countries such as Japan or the United States.

The last published status updates for Indigo West indicated a repair timeframe in the first part of September.

stories.title: Macquarie passes on Stack Infra's $28b-plus data centres as bids land
stories.summary: Macquarie has declined to participate in the sale process for Stack Infrastructure's Asia-Pacific data centre portfolio, valued at more than A$28 billion, as formal bids from other suitors are submitted. The decision removes one of the most prominent infrastructure investors from contention in what would rank among the region's largest-ever digital infrastructure transactions. Remaining bidders are now positioning offers for the hyperscale-focused platform.
stories.why_it_matters: Macquarie's exit narrows the field of deep-pocketed buyers and could reshape the pricing and structure of one of APAC's largest data centre deals, affecting valuations across the sector. For operators and investors, it signals that even the most active infrastructure funds are being selective about entry price amid rising build costs and interest-rate pressure.
stories.content:
Macquarie Asset Management did not submit an indicative offer for the Stack portfolio, multiple sources told Street Talk on the condition of anonymity. That’s despite it hiring two investment banks, UBS and Goldman Sachs, for advice on funding and diligence.

stories.title: Energy overtakes land as biggest data centre bottleneck
stories.summary: Industry executives and analysts report that securing power supply has replaced land acquisition as the primary constraint on data centre development across Asia-Pacific markets. Grid connection queues, limited substation capacity, and competition from electrification demand are delaying projects in key hubs even where sites are available. The shift is forcing developers to engage utilities earlier and to explore self-generation and alternative energy arrangements.
stories.why_it_matters: This marks a fundamental reordering of site-selection economics: markets once prized for cheap land and connectivity now win or lose projects on power availability. Developers, utilities, and governments face pressure to accelerate grid investment, while operators in power-constrained hubs risk multi-year delays that could redirect capacity growth toward emerging markets with more accessible energy.
